prize_parts.citation: For structural and mechanistic discoveries on nitrogenase, revealing how the iron-molybdenum cofactor binds and reduces dinitrogen in biological nitrogen fixation

statement.case_for: Nitrogenase is a single, well-defined achievement with a physically grounded mechanistic story. Rees's crystal structures of the MoFe protein and FeMo-cofactor, the interstitial carbide, and the recent cryo-EM turnover states make the chemistry visible. Dean's genetics and biochemistry made the protein tractable, and Seefeldt's kinetics and spectroscopy established the electron-transfer and ATP-coupling cycle. The work has been confirmed by several independent groups over about three decades and bears directly on the nitrogen cycle and on ammonia synthesis. This is the kind of electron, proton and substrate-binding mechanism in a biological system that a chemistry prize should recognise, and it is attributable to a small group.
statement.case_against: The mechanism of N2 reduction at the cofactor is still not settled, and the catalytic intermediates are debated. A citation could therefore be read as rewarding structures more than mechanism. Attribution among Rees, Dean, Seefeldt, Einsle and Ribbe is hard under the three-person limit, and any trio will leave out a contributor with a serious claim. I also hold this view partly because it matches my own interests in biological energy conversion, and I should not mistake that for evidence of consensus merit.

responses.point: Zou ranks B009 second and proposes Rees, Einsle and Seefeldt, since the crystallographic advances (cofactor structure, carbide, ligand-bound states) carry the evidential weight, while noting the catalytic mechanism is still incompletely resolved and so may be early.
responses.response: I agree that the structural core is the strongest evidence and that the mechanism is incomplete. We differ on the third name. Einsle's atomic-resolution structure and carbide assignment are decisive for the cofactor composition, but Dean's genetics and biochemistry made the isolation and the Rees structural work possible, and his work on cofactor biosynthesis and mutant analysis runs through the whole field. I would want the expert reports to show how much of the carbide and ligand-bound-state advance is Einsle's alone rather than shared with Rees. I do not think the citation should rest on the unresolved substrate-binding step, so I would word it around structure and cofactor chemistry and not claim the full catalytic cycle.

responses.point: Aili ranks B068 first with Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli, arguing that induced-proximity degradation is a new design principle for undruggable targets and that, although no PROTAC is approved, the independent confirmation and breadth of adoption make recognition defensible.
responses.response: I accept that the PROTAC concept is original and has been taken up widely. My reservation is timing and attribution. Without an approved degrader, the evidence that the concept works in patients is incomplete, and the molecular-glue branch (Handa, Ito, Gray, Sakamoto, Kim) has partly separate credit. Your own opening and Chabes's both admit that any three-name split excludes a major contributor, and I would not want the prize to depend on that choice. I treat nitrogenase as more settled. The structures have survived replication by several groups for decades, whereas the degrader story is still mainly a clinical promise.

responses.point: Sparr ranks B003 first, arguing that phase separation is a thermodynamic concept linking soft-matter physics to cell biology, with fifteen years of confirmation and so timely recognition.
responses.response: I respect the physical-chemistry foundation, and I rank B003 fourth. But I do not agree that more than fifteen years of work makes it mature. Aqvist and Linke both note that which condensates are truly phase-separated in vivo remains debated, and overexpression and in vitro artefacts have not been fully cleared. The attribution among Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen, Pappu and Mittag is also a real five-way problem. I would want the expert reports to separate the demonstrated physical principle from the biological claims before treating it as ready.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks B024 first, calling base editing a genuinely new chemical tool that is already in clinical trials, with Liu as the decisive driver and Komor and Gaudelli as the key experimentalists, but flags the Kondo and Nishida priority question.
responses.response: Base editing is a clear invention and I rank it seventh despite the adoption it has already had. Two questions remain for me. First, the Kondo and Nishida Target-AID work was parallel, and I cannot resolve priority from the supplied credit. Second, the chemistry is engineered deaminases and protein evolution on DNA, which sits close to the 2020 CRISPR prize and to the 2018 directed-evolution prize. If we pick it, I would want the citation to state precisely what is chemically new. Your point that clinical safety data are still limited also applies here.

uncertainties: Allocation among Rees, Dean, Seefeldt, Einsle and Ribbe, and whether the expert reports support Einsle ahead of Dean.
Whether the unresolved catalytic intermediates make a mechanism-based citation premature, so that the wording should be limited to structure and cofactor chemistry.
Whether the committee sees nitrogenase as sufficiently distinct from earlier recognition of structural biology and bioinorganic work.
I am relying on recalled literature and have not verified priority details independently.
statement.conflict_note: I work on proton transfer in cytochrome c oxidase, a different enzyme from nitrogenase, and the provided profile shows no collaboration with any B009 candidate. Xiaodong Zou is my Stockholm University colleague, which does not bear on any shortlisted candidate. No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile.
